findings.title: Classical signature (ECDSA P-256): future quantum risk
findings.detail: The server proves its identity with ECDSA P-256, which a quantum computer will be able to forge. This is not "harvest now, decrypt later": a signature only has to hold during the handshake, so the risk starts the day such a computer exists, not before. It does not limit today's security grade; in quantum readiness (model 2026.3), a post-quantum certificate would add 15 points.
findings.remediation: Nothing to do on the signature yet. Keep renewal automated so you can switch to ML-DSA or hybrid certificates as soon as authorities issue them.

findings.title: A single hybrid group
findings.detail: Only X25519MLKEM768 is accepted. It is the group browsers use, so the risk is low, but clients that require NIST curves (FIPS environments) cannot negotiate a post-quantum exchange.
findings.remediation: If you serve clients in regulated environments, add SecP256r1MLKEM768 to the group list. It depends on the server software: OpenSSL 3.5+ (and nginx or Apache built with it) accepts it in the group list (Groups / ssl_ecdh_curve); Caddy 2.11 does not accept that name in its curves directive yet; on a CDN or load balancer, it depends on its post-quantum settings.

findings.title: AES-128 and Grover's algorithm
findings.detail: The connection uses TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256. In theory Grover's algorithm reduces AES-128 to about 64-bit security, but it does not parallelize in practice and NIST still considers AES-128 adequate. Informational: it neither adds nor takes away on either axis.

findings.title: Certificate Transparency
findings.detail: The certificate carries SCTs: 2 embedded by the authority and 0 delivered in the handshake. Informational.

findings.title: Automated renewal (Let's Encrypt)
findings.detail: The certificate is issued by Let's Encrypt, an authority that works through ACME (automatic renewal; 89-day validity). Switching to post-quantum certificates should be just another update.

findings.title: Post-quantum key exchange: X25519MLKEM768
findings.detail: With a current browser's offer, the server negotiates the hybrid group X25519MLKEM768 (classical + ML-KEM, FIPS 203). Traffic captured today stays protected even if a quantum computer breaks the classical part ("harvest now, decrypt later").

findings.title: TLS 1.3 available
findings.detail: TLS 1.3 is the current protocol version and the only one where hybrid post-quantum groups exist.

findings.title: Valid certificate
findings.detail: The chain is trusted, matches the name and is current (issuer: Let's Encrypt; expires in 81 days).

findings.title: Forward secrecy
findings.detail: Every connection uses an ephemeral key exchange: even if the server's private key leaked, it would not decrypt past connections.

findings.title: Sound TLS 1.3 suites
findings.detail: Every TLS 1.3 suite accepted uses authenticated encryption with a full-size tag: TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256, TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384, TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256.

not_evaluated.label: PSK, SRP, Kerberos and GOST suites (they need credentials or algorithms a scanner does not have)
